clue.text: Voice coach providing fast online service?

parts.note: to voice an opinion is to express it
to coach a pupil or a team is to train them

explanation.surface: A singing teacher offers quick lessons over the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Online' is not the internet here: read it as 'on line', a service running on a railway line, which the question mark admits is a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: a quick railway service runs on a line, so it is literally 'on-line'.

clue.text: Run into bar for scrap?

indicators.note: into says the first piece goes inside the word that follows it

parts.note: bar as a preposition means except, as in 'all bar one'
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone dashes into a pub hoping for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts R inside EXCEPT. The surface suggests a pub brawl, but 'bar' is the preposition and 'scrap' is a small piece, here a passage taken from a longer text.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose example: a short passage lifted from a book or speech is a fragment of it.

clue.text: Movement that's attractive to prey?

parts.note: the letters of 'to prey' are those of a word for verse, rearranged; a crossword clue for them could use a phrase meaning 'moving' as its anagram signal after that word

explanation.surface: A predator's graceful stalking that fascinates its victim.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'to prey' is what you get when the first word of the answer is set moving, so the answer itself reads as a clue for those two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for something that moves with great grace and beauty, such as a dancer or athlete.

clue.text: Begrudge diplomat dropping round

indicators.note: dropping says the diplomat word loses the letter that follows

parts.note: an envoy is a diplomatic representative
the letter O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Resent an ambassador who gets out of buying his turn of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to resent someone's good fortune is to covet it jealously.

clue.text: Way cats exercise?

parts.note: a way is a street, abbreviated ST
to cat is old slang for to vomit, so 'cats' as a verb is retches

explanation.surface: The manner in which felines keep themselves supple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cats' is not the animal but a slang verb meaning vomits. The whole clue also hints at the answer, since cats famously arch and extend themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: limbering-up moves that extend the muscles are a kind of physical workout.

clue.text: I get up after I serve sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches says the words before it hold the answer between their outer letters, as bread holds a filling

explanation.surface: A host leaves the table once the sandwiches have been handed round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like the food being served, but it is a verb: 'after I serve' contains the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Description in the first person: someone who gets out of bed, as in 'early bird'.

clue.text: Can I turn clergyman out?

indicators.note: turn tells you to turn round the two words before it, reading them from the end to the start

parts.note: taken as written
a curate is a junior clergyman assisting a parish priest

explanation.surface: A parishioner asks whether the vicar can be evicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reads the first two words backwards to give INAC. The tiny last word is the definition: a figure that is 'out' is wrong, as in 'out by ten pounds'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the sense of mistaken: a calculation that is wrong by some amount is said to be out.

clue.text: Zone de Paris sans metro et diner nouveau

indicators.note: nouveau is French for new, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French description of a Paris district with no underground, and a new place to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is in French; 'nouveau' rearranges SANS METRO and DINER, with 'et' only joining them. Paris is divided into twenty of these numbered districts.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the French capital is split into twenty numbered administrative districts with this name.

clue.text: Country garden in Cornwall?

parts.note: Cornwall is the county at the far south-west tip of England, so something there is in the SW
Eden is the biblical garden; the Eden Project is also a famous garden attraction in Cornwall

explanation.surface: A rural plot of flowers in England's far south-west.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eden Project, huge greenhouse domes in a former clay pit, is in Cornwall, England's south-western county, so it is whimsically a south-west garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Scandinavian kingdom is one nation among many.

clue.text: Far from stupid to carry a knife

indicators.note: to carry says the first word holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: someone far from stupid is clever

explanation.surface: It is a sensible precaution to have a blade on you.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a butcher's heavy chopping blade is one kind of this tool.

clue.text: Pirate's fight to keep boat moving

definitions.note: the possessive is only the surface; the definition is the pirate himself

parts.note: to spar is to fight, especially in boxing practice
to row is to propel a boat with oars

explanation.surface: A buccaneer struggles to keep his ship under way.
explanation.walkthrough: The pirate is Captain Jack, Johnny Depp's character in the Pirates of the Caribbean films.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by name: Captain Jack of the Pirates of the Caribbean films has this surname.

clue.text: Still red, like gold dust

definitions.meaning: a steak cooked only briefly stays red inside
something 'like gold dust' is very hard to find

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: lightly cooked meat, and scarce like something precious.

clue.text: Shower unit with flashy components?

parts.note: read as weather rather than plumbing: a single mass in the sky that produces rain, with lightning as its 'flashy' parts

explanation.surface: A bathroom fitting with showy chrome parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsical description: a dark thundery mass in the sky delivers rain and lightning flashes.

clue.text: Author's praise, or otherwise, for manager

parts.note: the author is the setter speaking, and 'author's' as 'author is' becomes I'm

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the two words before it are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer's approval or disapproval of the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or otherwise' looks like a set phrase, but 'or' is part of the fodder: 'otherwise' rearranges PRAISE OR into PRESARIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: someone who organises and runs theatrical or musical shows manages them.

clue.text: Victorious pilot adopting uniform speed

indicators.note: adopting says the pilot word takes the other pieces inside itself

parts.note: a pilot is a trial run, as a pilot episode or pilot scheme
Uniform is the radio alphabet word for U
mph, miles per hour, is the unit in which speed is measured in Britain

explanation.surface: A winning airman settles on a steady velocity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform speed' reads as one phrase but is two separate pieces taken in by 'adopting', and the pilot is a test run rather than an airman.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: celebrating a win, as in a conqueror's procession or arch.

clue.text: Being one-dimensional, I approach thing in empty lobby

indicators.note: in says the three pieces before it sit inside what follows
empty removes the contents of the next word, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: to approach is to near, as a ship nears port
it is a pronoun for a thing

explanation.surface: A shallow person walks up to an object in a deserted hotel foyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: the quality of running along a single straight line, which has one dimension only.

clue.text: Sculptor's endless chipping away

definitions.note: the possessive is only the surface; the definition is the sculptor himself

indicators.note: endless here strips both ends, the first and last letters, from the word for chipping away

parts.note: eroding is gradually wearing or chipping away

explanation.surface: A stone carver hammers at the block without ever stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' takes the first and last letters, E and G, off ERODING. The answer is the French artist who made The Thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by name: Auguste, the Frenchman who made The Thinker and The Kiss.

clue.text: Bone made of iron — strange, on reflection

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: on reflection says the word before it is seen as in a mirror, back to front

parts.note: rum is an old British word for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A skeleton part cast in metal seems odd when you think about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns RUM, old British slang for odd, into MUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the thigh's long supporting part of the skeleton.

clue.text: Flat edge of tart reaching edges of glassware

parts.note: a flan is an open pastry tart

indicators.note: edges of picks the first and last letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: The level rim of a pastry touches the sides of the dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a projecting rim on a pipe or wheel, used for strength or attachment.

clue.text: "Impure" is, instead, "pure"

indicators.note: something impure is mixed or adulterated, so the letters that follow are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A proofreader notes that a word marked as unclean should read the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impure' is the anagram signal, rearranging IS and INSTEAD; the commas hide that 'is' is fodder, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: something cleaned of germs and dirt has been made clean and wholesome.

clue.text: Boozer's body found in squat, covered in refuse

indicators.note: covered in says the squat word is wrapped by the word that follows

parts.note: to refuse is to deny, as in denying a request
to squat is to sit on one's haunches

explanation.surface: A drunk's corpse is discovered in an occupied building, buried under rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is the verb that 'covered in' wraps round the squat, not rubbish; the body is the fullness or thickness of a drink, with 'boozer' whimsically the booze.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose sense: the weight or thickness of an alcoholic drink is what tasters call its body.

clue.text: Disruptive Italians worried about army officer

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters go round the officer
worried means agitated, so the letters of the word before it are agitated into a new order

parts.note: OC is the military abbreviation for Officer Commanding

explanation.surface: Unruly people from Italy are anxious over a military man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italians are not the troublemakers but the letters that 'worried' stirs into ANTISIAL, which 'about' then splits round the officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: behaviour that upsets and annoys the people around is described this way.

clue.text: Don't go — start to tame reindeer

parts.note: the opposite of go is come, so 'don't go' suggests come

indicators.note: start to picks the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to stay and begin training a deer.
explanation.walkthrough: One of Santa's sleigh team in the poem 'A Visit from St Nicholas', alongside Dasher, Dancer and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by name: one of the eight that pull Santa's sleigh in the Christmas poem.

clue.text: Piercing cry

definitions.meaning: a piercing wind or wit is sharp and cutting
to wail in grief, as mourners do at an Irish wake

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: sharp and cutting as an adjective, and to wail in lament as a verb.

clue.text: Something like headless body

indicators.note: headless removes the first letter, the head, of the body word

parts.note: the torso is the trunk of the body

explanation.surface: An object resembling a decapitated corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym phrase for approximately: 'something like fifty' and 'fifty, roughly' say the same.

clue.text: Fabric is not the hardest stuff to pack

parts.note: grog is rum watered down, so not the strongest ('hardest') liquor
to pack something in tightly is to ram it

explanation.surface: Cloth turns out to be fairly easy material to put in a suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard stuff' is strong drink, so watered-down navy rum is 'not the hardest'. The answer is a coarse cloth of silk and mohair.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a coarse cloth of silk and mohair, often stiffened with gum.

clue.text: National airlines flying out of Norway

indicators.note: flying means moving about in the air, so the letters of the word before it move about
out of says the letter for the country named next is taken away

parts.note: N is the international vehicle code for Norway

explanation.surface: State-owned carriers operate flights departing from Scandinavia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' removes N from AIRLINES and 'flying' rearranges the remaining AIRLIES. 'National' is a noun here: a citizen of a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a citizen of one particular Middle Eastern state is a national of it.

clue.text: How one may see guts of crippled patient?

wordplay.reading: P P, the music mark for quietly, twice

parts.words: How one may see guts of crippled
parts.note: the middle two letters of 'crippled' are P and P, and p in music stands for piano, meaning quietly or gently; seen that way the pair reads as that instruction given twice

explanation.surface: A grim way of viewing an injured person's insides in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guts of' picks the middle letters PP of crippled; each P is the musical marking for playing quietly. 'Patient' is the adjective, not a hospital case.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: a cautious, unhurried approach, from the proverb about catching a monkey.
